# session-search

Searches session transcripts: an SQLite full-text index, grep, and semantic search by embeddings.

- **Runs in:** the harness process
- **Source:** [lisp/modules/harness-session-search.el](../../lisp/modules/harness-session-search.el)
- **Loaded:** when enabled (see `harness-enable-modules`)
- **Requires:** [store](store.md), [session](session.md)
- **Required by:** [tasks-search](tasks-search.md)

## About

One search over the transcripts of every session, for the
`session_search` tool, the task board's search and the UI's
`harness-search-sessions`.

The transcripts stay where they are, in the node logs
(sessions/ID.nodes.jsonl).  This module keeps an index of them in
SQLite: search.db, beside usage.db in the state directory, with a row
per node holding its readable text, and an FTS5 full-text index over
the rows.  The index is a cache.  Deleting search.db loses nothing:
it is built again from the logs, and `session/search-rebuild` does
that on demand.  It is a database of its own, not tables in usage.db,
because it grows about as large as the logs, while usage.db is small
and holds what nothing can rebuild.

Keeping it current.  The index remembers how far it has read each log
(a byte offset), so bringing a session up to date reads only the
lines appended since.  An update line (the final text of a streamed
reply, a changed `:meta`) is merged into the row of its node, so the
whole of every reply is searchable: grep over the logs sees only what
one line holds, and missed everything a reply streamed after its
first chunk.  Nodes are indexed shortly after they are written
(`session/node-added`, `session/node-updated`, `session/forked`); a
search first catches up with the logs that grew since; and the logs
never indexed are read in the background, a slice of a few tens of
milliseconds at a time, newest session first (`run-at-time`: the
harness process has no idle time).  A deleted session's rows go with
it, in the background too.

Modes (OPTS `:mode` of `session/search`):
- `text` (the default): full-text search.  A word matches whole words
  in any form ("parse" finds "parsing", porter stemming; case and
  accents are ignored), every word must match, "quoted words" match as
  a phrase, word* matches a prefix, OR between words matches either
  and -word excludes.  Best match first (BM25): each session is
  ranked by its best node, fused (reciprocal rank fusion) with the
  sessions whose name has the words and, when an embedding model is
  set, with how near in meaning they are.  When no session has every
  word, those with some of them come back, marked `:loose`; when
  none has any, the nearest in meaning, when there are vectors --
  those nearly as near as the nearest -- and the result says so
  (`:note`).
- `literal` and `regexp`: the text as given, or an extended regular
  expression as grep -E reads it, matched case-insensitively by grep
  over the logs, newest session first.  Update lines count: a node
  matches on the text it has in the end.
- `semantic`: nearest in meaning only, by the vectors of the
  embedding model (`harness-session-search-embedding-model`).
Without SQLite or FTS5, with `harness-session-search-index` off, or
while most of the logs a search covers are still to be indexed, text
mode falls back to grep for the text as typed, and the result says so
(`:note`).

Embeddings are off unless `harness-session-search-embedding-model`
names a model of a provider that embeds (`provider/embed`): an
OpenAI-compatible endpoint (OpenAI, OpenRouter, or a local Ollama,
LM Studio, llama.cpp or vLLM server), say
"openai:text-embedding-3-small".  Then the text of user messages,
replies, plans and compaction summaries is cut into chunks, embedded
in batches in the background, newest first, and stored as int8
vectors keyed by the hash of their chunk, so text met twice (the
history a fork copies) is embedded once.  A search embeds its query
and compares it with every vector, in Elisp, with integer arithmetic:
a fraction of a second for tens of thousands of chunks.  Changing the
model drops the vectors and embeds everything again.  The text goes to
the model's provider, which is why it is the user's choice; the
allowed models of the policy hold for it (`harness-allowed-models`),
and in corporate mode only a server on this machine embeds.

Secrets.  The index holds a copy of the readable text of every
transcript, so a secret that got into one is in it too: in the rows, in
the full-text index built over them, and in the vectors of the chunks
that held it.  Deleting or changing a row does not take its text out
of the file.  FTS5 keeps the words of a deleted row until its segments
are merged; SQLite keeps the pages it freed, and the write-ahead log
the older versions of pages, until they are reused or the file is
written again.  Three methods deal with that, for the redaction of the
harness (see harness-redaction.el), which redacts the logs themselves:

- `session/search-redact` scans the rows for secrets, counting and
  naming no text; or, once the logs were redacted, forgets the rows of
  the sessions it is given and reads their logs again from their start.
  The index is never edited in place: a row's text is only ever what
  its log says.  A secret is a bound parameter of the queries, never
  part of their text, and nothing here logs it.
- `session/search-purge` then takes the old text out of the file: it
  drops the rows of sessions that no longer exist and the vectors no
  chunk uses any more (a vector is derived from the text of its chunk),
  merges the FTS5 segments (the `optimize` command, which drops deleted
  terms), VACUUMs the database and empties the write-ahead log
  (`wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`).  Given the secrets, it counts their
  bytes in the three files of the index, and the terms FTS5 makes of
  them (it stores words lowercased and split at punctuation, so a
  secret with capitals is never in its pages as it was written), none
  of which is there when it worked.  The merge is what removes the
  dead terms from the live pages of the index: a VACUUM only copies
  them.
- `session/search-rebuild` drops the tables and makes them again, then
  VACUUMs and empties the log too, so an index built anew does not
  leave the old text in the file it was dropped from.

A VACUUM writes the whole database again.  For a large search.db it
blocks the harness process, which does nothing else meanwhile, for a
while (seconds to minutes), and it needs free disk space for a copy of
the database in the temporary directory and the same again in the
write-ahead log.  Rebuilding is much cheaper than purging a large
index, as the VACUUM then finds nothing to copy, but it indexes every
log again in the background, and embeds it again when there is an
embedding model.

## Provides

### Methods

- `session/search` (query &optional opts) — Search the transcripts and names of sessions for QUERY; return a promise.
- `session/search-purge` (&optional secrets) — Take the text the index dropped out of its files, and return a plist.
- `session/search-rebuild` — Drop the search index and build it again from the logs, in the background.
- `session/search-redact` (ids secrets &optional dry-run) — Find SECRETS in the search index, or index again after they left the logs.
- `session/search-status` — Return the state of the search index as a plist.

### Options

- `harness-session-search-embedding-dimensions` — Length of the vectors to ask the embedding model for, or nil for its own.
- `harness-session-search-embedding-model` — Model that embeds session text for semantic search, as PROVIDER:NAME, or nil.
- `harness-session-search-index` — Non-nil keeps a full-text index of the session transcripts, in search.db.

## Uses

### Methods it calls

- `provider/embed` ([provider](provider.md)), when it is loaded
- `session/exists-p` ([session](session.md))
- `session/list` ([session](session.md))
- `session/node` ([session](session.md))
- `store/sqlite` ([store](store.md))
- `usage/price` ([usage](usage.md)), when it is loaded
- `usage/record` ([usage](usage.md)), when it is loaded

### Events it handles

- `session/deleted` → `harness-session-search--on-deleted`
- `session/forked` → `harness-session-search--on-forked`
- `session/node-added` → `harness-session-search--on-written`
- `session/node-updated` → `harness-session-search--on-node-updated`
